meta.title: Wealth Management & 401(k) FAQs | PointOak
meta.description: Answers to common questions about wealth management, financial planning, investments, retirement, 401(k) consulting, fiduciary services, fees, and working with PointOak.

blocks.text: Financial decisions can get complicated quickly, whether you're managing your family's wealth or overseeing an employer-sponsored retirement plan. We've organized the questions we hear most often into categories so you can quickly find what you're looking for. If your question isn't answered here, we're happy to talk through it with you.

items.q: Who does PointOak work with?

a.text: PointOak serves two primary groups: individuals and families seeking private wealth management and financial planning, and businesses responsible for employer-sponsored retirement plans.

items.q: Where is PointOak located?

a.text: PointOak is headquartered in McLean, Virginia and serves clients throughout the DC Metro area and nationwide, subject to applicable regulatory requirements.

items.q: Is the initial consultation complimentary?

a.text: Yes. The initial consultation is complimentary and is an opportunity to discuss your goals, questions, and whether our services may be a good fit.

items.q: What does fee-only mean?

a.text: PointOak is compensated by clients for the advisory and consulting services we provide. We do not receive investment-product commissions. A fee-only compensation structure can reduce certain conflicts associated with product sales, although no compensation model eliminates every potential conflict.

items.q: Is PointOak a fiduciary?

a.text: PointOak is an SEC-registered investment adviser and serves its advisory clients as a fiduciary. We are required to act in our clients’ best interests and put their interests ahead of our own. For retirement plans, PointOak may also provide services as a 3(21) investment fiduciary or 3(38) investment manager.

items.q: Is every financial advisor always a fiduciary?

a.text: Standards can vary based on the services being provided and the capacity in which a financial professional is acting. Some professionals may act as fiduciaries in certain relationships but not others. Clients should understand the capacity, compensation structure, and potential conflicts associated with a relationship.

items.q: What is wealth management?

a.text: Wealth management brings investment management and financial planning together across investments, retirement, income needs, taxes, workplace benefits, Social Security and pensions, estate considerations, and other major financial decisions.
segs: and financial planning together across investments, retirement, income needs, taxes, workplace benefits, Social Security and pensions, estate considerations, and other major financial decisions.

items.q: Is there a minimum account size?

a.text: PointOak’s wealth-management relationships vary based on the services needed, portfolio size, complexity, and overall circumstances. The complimentary initial consultation is an opportunity to discuss your goals and determine whether our services are a good fit.

items.q: How does PointOak charge for private wealth management?

a.text: PointOak is fee-only. Ongoing investment management is generally charged as an asset-based advisory fee that varies by account size and scope. Comprehensive financial planning may be included or provided through a separate engagement. Specific fees are discussed before engagement.

items.q: How does PointOak manage portfolios?

a.text: Portfolio recommendations consider goals, time horizon, risk, income needs, tax considerations, and the broader financial plan. Our process can include strategic asset allocation, investment selection, monitoring, rebalancing, and tax-aware management.

items.q: Does PointOak use proprietary investments?

a.text: No. PointOak uses an open-architecture approach and is not limited to a proprietary investment family.

items.q: Does PointOak use alternative investments?

a.text: For appropriate clients, PointOak may evaluate alternative and private-market investments. These strategies can involve limited liquidity, longer holding periods, valuation complexity, higher fees, leverage, and eligibility requirements and are not appropriate for every client or portfolio.

items.q: Should I roll over an old 401(k)?

a.text: It depends. Depending on the plan and your circumstances, your options may include leaving assets in your former employer’s plan, moving eligible assets to a new employer’s plan, rolling assets to an IRA, or taking a distribution. Fees, investment options, services, withdrawal rules, creditor protections, tax considerations, and your broader financial strategy should all be considered before deciding.

items.q: What is the difference between a rollover and a Roth conversion?

a.text: A rollover generally moves assets between eligible retirement accounts or plans. A Roth conversion changes pre-tax retirement assets to Roth assets and generally creates taxable income in the year of conversion.

items.q: When might a Roth conversion make sense?

a.text: Potential opportunities can arise during lower-income years, before required minimum distributions begin, or when other planning circumstances make paying tax today worth evaluating. The analysis should also consider Medicare premiums, Social Security taxation, and other tax consequences.

items.q: Can a plan sponsor outsource fiduciary responsibilities?

a.text: Certain fiduciary functions can be delegated to qualified service providers, but the appointing fiduciary generally retains responsibility for prudently selecting and monitoring those providers.

items.q: How often should a retirement plan be reviewed?

a.text: Ongoing fiduciary oversight should occur regularly. The appropriate cadence depends on the topic, plan circumstances, and governance process.

items.q: What does a 3(21) investment fiduciary do?

a.text: A 3(21) investment fiduciary provides investment advice and recommendations, while the plan sponsor or committee retains final decision-making authority.

items.q: What does a 3(38) investment manager do?

a.text: A 3(38) investment manager has discretionary authority over designated investment decisions within the delegated scope. The appointing fiduciary retains responsibility for prudently selecting and monitoring the manager.

items.q: What is the primary difference?

a.text: 3(21): PointOak recommends; the committee decides. 3(38): PointOak makes designated investment decisions under delegated authority.

items.q: How often should plan fees be benchmarked?

a.text: PointOak generally conducts a full plan and provider benchmark every three to five years, or sooner when circumstances warrant. In years when we are not conducting a full benchmark, we perform a fee benchmark and work with the provider to reprice the plan annually. The three-to-five-year interval is PointOak's practice, not a DOL or ERISA requirement.

items.q: Does benchmarking mean choosing the cheapest provider?

a.text: No. Fees should be evaluated in relation to the services, investments, technology, participant support, and other value provided. The lowest-cost option is not automatically the most appropriate option.

items.q: Can participants meet individually with PointOak?

a.text: Yes. PointOak can offer participants complimentary 30-minute individual consultations to discuss questions related to their retirement plan and broader retirement decisions. Depending on the engagement, topics may include contribution rates, investment allocation, pre-tax versus Roth contributions, beneficiaries, retirement readiness, and available options for eligible retirement assets. Any separate private-wealth or financial-planning relationship with PointOak is optional and subject to a separate engagement and applicable fees.

items.q: When should I start retirement income planning?

a.text: Planning before retirement provides time to evaluate income sources, investments, Social Security, healthcare, taxes, and withdrawal decisions. The appropriate timing depends on your circumstances; it is also useful to revisit the strategy after retirement begins.

items.q: Is retirement planning just about how much I've saved?

a.text: No. Accumulating assets is only part of retirement planning. As retirement approaches, you also need to determine how your savings, Social Security, pensions, and other resources will work together to support your spending needs.

items.q: Is the 4% rule a retirement income plan?

a.text: No. A withdrawal-rate rule can be a general reference point, but it does not replace an individualized analysis of taxes, account types, income sources, spending, investment risk, and the ability to adjust over time.

items.q: When should I claim Social Security?

a.text: An appropriate claiming strategy depends on your income needs, health and longevity expectations, other retirement assets, household circumstances, and survivor-benefit considerations. There is no single claiming age that's right for everyone.

items.q: Should I take a pension lump sum or monthly benefit?

a.text: It depends on the terms of your pension and your broader financial circumstances. We consider income needs, survivor benefits, investment risk, liquidity, longevity, and estate objectives before evaluating the available options.

items.q: Should Social Security and pension decisions be evaluated separately?

a.text: They should be considered together with the broader financial plan. Both can affect household cash flow, taxes, survivor income, and the amount needed from investments.

items.q: What is tax-efficient investing?

a.text: Tax-aware investing considers potential tax consequences alongside investment risk, diversification, liquidity, and other portfolio objectives. It does not mean minimizing current-year taxes at any cost.

items.q: Does PointOak prepare tax returns?

a.text: No. PointOak incorporates tax considerations into financial planning and investment management but does not prepare tax returns or replace your CPA or tax professional.

items.q: Why does asset location matter?

a.text: Different investments and account types can have different tax characteristics. Coordinating which investments are held in taxable, tax-deferred, and Roth accounts may improve after-tax efficiency, depending on the client's circumstances.

items.q: Does PointOak draft wills or trusts?

a.text: No. Estate attorneys prepare legal documents. PointOak coordinates financial accounts, beneficiary information, investments, and wealth-transfer considerations with your attorney and tax professionals.

items.q: Why should beneficiary designations be reviewed separately from my will?

a.text: Certain assets with valid beneficiary designations may pass according to those designations rather than under the terms of a will. Your attorney can advise how the applicable rules affect your situation.

items.q: Can PointOak help with RSUs, stock options, and deferred compensation?

a.text: Yes. We help executives evaluate equity compensation and deferred-compensation decisions within the context of taxes, diversification, investment strategy, and retirement timing.

items.q: What is an Investment Policy Statement?

a.text: An Investment Policy Statement, or IPS, provides a framework for selecting, monitoring, placing on watch, and replacing investments. It helps committees apply consistent criteria and document their process.

items.q: Is an IPS required by ERISA?

a.text: ERISA does not specifically require every plan to maintain an Investment Policy Statement. Many committees adopt one to guide investment oversight. The document should remain consistent with the plan's governing documents and applicable law, and its procedures should be followed and reviewed as appropriate.

items.q: Does poor short-term performance mean a fund should immediately be removed?

a.text: No. A prudent review considers the investment's role, risk, relevant benchmarks, fees, manager stability, philosophy, and style consistency rather than relying on recent returns alone.

items.q: What is an investment watchlist?

a.text: A watchlist identifies investments that warrant closer review under the plan's monitoring framework. Placement on watch is not an automatic instruction to replace the fund.

items.q: What is 401(k) plan design?

a.text: Plan design includes eligibility, employer matching and other contributions, automatic enrollment, automatic escalation, vesting, and other provisions that determine how a plan operates.

items.q: How often should plan design be reviewed?

a.text: PointOak generally recommends reviewing plan design annually and whenever significant organizational, workforce, regulatory, or plan changes occur. This is a recommended practice, not a universal legal deadline.

items.q: Do you consider what other employers in our industry offer?

a.text: Yes. Available industry and peer-plan information can provide context around matching formulas, employer contributions, eligibility, vesting, and automatic features. Those comparisons inform recommendations rather than determining the design by themselves.

items.q: Are all target date funds with the same year essentially the same?

a.text: No. Funds with the same target year can have different equity exposure, glide paths, fees, investment structures, and risk profiles.

items.q: What is a target date fund glide path?

a.text: The glide path describes how the fund's asset allocation changes as it approaches and moves beyond the target date.

items.q: What is the difference between a to and through glide path?

a.text: A to-retirement glide path generally reaches its most conservative allocation around the target date. A through-retirement approach continues changing allocation afterward. Neither is universally better. Analysis should consider underlying assumptions, participant demographics and behavior, plan objectives, fees, structure, and the expected role of the series.

items.q: Is a QDIA the same as a target date fund?

a.text: No. A target date fund may serve as a qualified default investment alternative, but the terms are not interchangeable. The plan's default strategy should be evaluated within the broader investment-menu and monitoring process.

items.q: What is PointOak's Virtual Fiduciary File?

a.text: The Virtual Fiduciary File is a centralized way to organize documentation created through the retirement-plan governance process, including investment reviews, committee records, fee benchmarks, and provider evaluations.

items.q: Does a Virtual Fiduciary File replace the recordkeeper?

a.text: No. The recordkeeper maintains participant and administrative records. The Virtual Fiduciary File focuses on the committee's governance and oversight documentation.

items.q: What should fiduciary documentation explain?

a.text: The record should show the information considered, alternatives evaluated, decisions made, rationale, and any follow-up responsibilities. Organized records support the process; they do not guarantee a particular regulatory or legal outcome.

items.title: You Don't Need to Have Everything Figured Out Before We Meet
